mainTopic: תשובה, the sin of the עגל and whether ישראל could have been free of death, and ה׳'s plea that ישראל keep the תורה
overview: This amud finishes the teaching that דוד's sin and the sin of the עגל came to show that תשובה works: an individual looks to דוד, and a community looks to the generation of the עגל. It then teaches that one מצוה walks ahead of a person into עולם הבא, while one עבירה clings to him like a dog. ריש לקיש says we should thank our ancestors for sinning, because otherwise they would have stayed like angels. The גמרא challenges this with many פסוקים. In the end it reads his words as 'it would be as if we had not come into the world', and it explains that the laws about death were written on condition. A ברייתא says death could never have been removed, but ריש לקיש follows רבי יוסי, who says the תורה would have freed ישראל from death. Along the way, the גמרא teaches that four people are considered like dead: a poor person, a blind person, a מצורע, and one without children. The amud closes with ברייתות that the 'if' of 'אם בחקתי' is ה׳ pleading, and that משה called ישראל ingrates for not answering 'You give it!' The proof from the מן continues on the next amud.

steps.title: An individual learns from דוד, a community learns from the עגל
steps.stepSummary: The teaching of רבי יהושע בן לוי ends here. A single sinner is pointed to דוד, and a sinning community is pointed to the generation of the עגל, as proof that תשובה works.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was to teach you: if one person sins, we tell him, 'Go look at the individual who sinned (דוד) and did תשובה.' If the community sins, we tell them, 'Go look at the community that sinned (the generation of the עגל) and did תשובה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the earlier statement of רבי יהושע בן לוי. It explains the purpose of the sins of דוד and of the עגל: they serve as models of תשובה for later people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי יהושע בן לוי said that neither דוד nor the generation of the עגל was the kind of people who would normally do such sins. Here he gives the reason it happened anyway. It gives two clear examples of תשובה, one for a single person and one for a whole community.

keyTerms.meaning: To teach you; this was meant to show you
The community, the public as a group
Go over to; go look at the example of

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not start a new teaching. It is the ending of רבי יהושע בן לוי's statement from just before, which explained why דוד and the generation of the עגל sinned.

phrases.english: To say to you,
that if an individual sinned —
we say to him: Go over to the individual,
phrases.notes: The 'individual' here is דוד, who sinned and did תשובה.

phrases.english: and if the community sinned —
we say to them: Go over to the community.
phrases.notes: The 'community' here is the generation of the עגל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the teaching of רבי יהושע בן לוי from the previous daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both a single sinner and a sinning community have a clear model showing that תשובה works: דוד for the individual, and the generation of the עגל for the community.

steps.title: Why both examples are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא uses a צריכא to show that neither example alone would be enough. Each case has a special feature that might seem to make תשובה easier only there.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both examples are needed. If we only had the individual, I might think he can do תשובה because his sin is not public, but a community whose sin is public cannot. If we only had the community, I might think they can do תשובה because they have many prayers, but an individual, whose merit is not as strong, cannot. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks itself why two examples are needed when one might seem enough. It shows that each example teaches something the other could not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An individual has an advantage: his sin is private. A community has a different advantage: many people are praying and asking for mercy. Each example alone could be explained by its own advantage, so both examples are needed. Together they show that תשובה works in every case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary; both teachings are needed
Their prayers for mercy are many

steps.whatToRemember: No sinner, private or public, alone or in a group, should think that תשובה is closed to him.

phrases.english: And it is necessary,
for if it had taught us only an individual —
that would be because his sin is not publicized,
but a community, whose sin is publicized —
I would say no.
And if it had taught us only a community —
that would be because their prayers for mercy are many,
but an individual, whose merit is not strong —
I would say no. So it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why step 1 needed two separate examples.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each example of תשובה covers a case the other cannot. Together they show that תשובה is open to both individuals and communities.

steps.title: דוד raised up the yoke of תשובה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings support from רבי שמואל בר נחמני in the name of רבי יונתן. He reads the פסוק 'הֻקַם עָל' to mean that דוד raised up the yoke of תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This matches what רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: What does the פסוק mean, 'The saying of דוד son of ישי, and the saying of the man raised on high'? It means: the saying of דוד son of ישי, who raised up the yoke of תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק, explained by רבי יונתן, that fits with what was just taught. דוד is described as the one who 'raised up' תשובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word עָל in the פסוק is read like עוֹל, meaning 'yoke.' דוד did not only do תשובה for himself. He set up תשובה as an example for everyone after him. This supports רבי יהושע בן לוי's idea that a single sinner is sent to look at דוד.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is the same as; this fits with
What is the meaning of what is written
The saying of, the words of

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that דוד's story is meant to be a lasting lesson that anyone can return.

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"The saying of David son of Yishai
and the saying of the man raised on high"?
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 23:1. The word עָל is being read like עוֹל, 'yoke.'

phrases.english: The saying of David son of Yishai,
who raised up the yoke of repentance.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a פסוק-based teaching that supports step 1's idea of דוד as the model of תשובה.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that דוד serves as the model of תשובה for individuals.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יונתן's reading of 'הֻקַם עָל' (שמואל ב 23:1) as 'raised up the yoke of תשובה.'

steps.title: A מצוה walks before you and an עבירה wraps around you
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds another teaching from the same chain of rabbis. One מצוה goes ahead of a person into עולם הבא, and one עבירה wraps around him and leads him to יום הדין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני also said in the name of רבי יונתן: Whoever does one מצוה in this world, it goes ahead of him and walks before him into עולם הבא, as it says, 'Your righteousness shall go before you, the glory of ה׳ shall gather you in.' Whoever does one עבירה, it wraps around him and leads him to יום הדין, as it says, 'The paths of their way wind around them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another teaching from the same chain of rabbis, רבי שמואל בר נחמני in the name of רבי יונתן. It teaches how one's actions stay with a person into the next world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a single מצוה has lasting power. It goes ahead of the person and leads the way into עולם הבא. A single עבירה also stays with the person: it 'wraps around' him (the word ילפתו sounds like מלפפתו) and brings him to judgment. Each claim is supported by its own פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: It wraps around him, clings to him

steps.whatToRemember: Every single action counts. One מצוה leads a person into עולם הבא, and one עבירה clings to him until judgment, which is why תשובה matters so much.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
Anyone who does one מצוה
in this world,
it goes ahead of him and walks before him
to the World to Come,
as it says: "And your righteousness shall go before you,
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 58:8

phrases.english: the glory of the Lord shall gather you in."
And anyone who commits one transgression,
it wraps around him and leads him
to the Day of Judgment,
as it says: "The paths of their way wind around, etc."
phrases.notes: איוב 6:18. The word יִלָּפְתוּ sounds like מְלַפַּפְתּוֹ, 'wraps around him.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another teaching from the same chain of rabbis named in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One מצוה goes before a person into עולם הבא, and one עבירה clings to him and leads him to יום הדין.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: A sin is tied to a person like a dog
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר adds that a sin stays tied to the sinner like a dog. He brings a פסוק about יוסף that hints the sinner stays with the sin even in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: The sin is tied to him like a dog, as it says: "And he did not listen to her, to lie by her, to be with her." "To lie by her" means in עולם הזה. "To be with her" means in עולם הבא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives his own picture of how an עבירה follows a person, adding to the teaching in Step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said a sin wraps around a person and leads him to יום הדין. רבי אלעזר goes further: the sin is tied to him like a dog on a leash and never leaves. He reads the two parts of the פסוק as two worlds: sinning here would have meant being stuck with her there.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar says:
It is tied to him like a dog,
phrases.notes: "It" is the sin, the one עבירה from the last teaching.

phrases.english: as it is stated:
"And he did not listen to her,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 39:10

phrases.english: "to lie by her, to be with her."
"To lie by her" means in this world,
"to be with her" means in the World to Come.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: קְשׁוּרָה בּוֹ כְּכֶלֶב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, stronger picture of how an עבירה follows a person, after the teaching in Step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sin stays tied to the sinner like a dog, even into עולם הבא.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: Thank our ancestors for sinning
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says we should be grateful to the generation of the עגל. If they had not sinned, they would have been like angels, and we would never have been born.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: Come, let us thank our ancestors. If they had not sinned, we would not have come into the world. As it says: "I said: You are godlike beings, and all of you are sons of the Most High." Once you ruined your deeds: "Yet you shall die like a man."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new and surprising teaching from ריש לקיש about the sin of the עגל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After מתן תורה, the people were on the level of angels ("אלהים אתם"), meaning they would live forever and not have children. Only after the sin did they become normal people who die ("כאדם תמותון"), and so they also had children. Since we come from those children, our existence depends on that sin.

keyTerms.meaning: if not for / had it not been

steps.confusionAlert: ריש לקיש is not praising the sin itself. He is pointing out that our being born came as a result of it.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Come and let us be grateful to our ancestors,
phrases.notes: He means the generation that sinned with the עגל.

phrases.english: for had they not sinned,
we would not have come into the world,
as it is stated:
"I said: You are godlike beings,"
phrases.notes: תהלים 82:6

phrases.english: "and all of you sons of the Most High."
Once you ruined your deeds:
"Yet you shall die like a man, etc."
phrases.notes: תהלים 82:7

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: בּוֹאוּ וְנַחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the sin of the עגל, mentioned in Step 1, and opens a new idea about it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without the sin of the עגל, the people would have been like angels with no children, so we would not exist.

steps.title: Challenge: But there was already a command to have children
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: Would they really not have had children? The Torah already commanded פרו ורבו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that if they had not sinned, they would not have had children? But it is written: "And you, be fruitful and multiply."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש with a פסוק commanding people to have children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש said that without the sin there would be no children. But the Torah told נח and his sons "פרו ורבו," so having children seems to be part of ה׳'s plan no matter what.

phrases.english: Is this to say that if they had not sinned
they would not have had children?
But isn't it written: "And you, be fruitful and multiply"!
phrases.notes: בראשית 9:7

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּאִי לָא חָטְאוּ לָא הֲווֹ מוֹלְדוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks ריש לקיש's claim from Step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's claim that without the sin there would be no children
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah commands פרו ורבו, so having children must have been planned anyway.

steps.title: Answer: That command lasted only until Sinai
steps.stepSummary: The command of פרו ורבו was meant for the time before סיני. At סיני the people would have become like angels.
steps.simpleTranslation: Until סיני.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in two words: the command to have children applied only until סיני.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At מתן תורה the people rose to the level of angels. Without the sin, they would have stayed there, and the old command to have children would no longer apply to them.

phrases.english: Until Sinai.
phrases.notes: He means פרו ורבו was in force only until מתן תורה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the time the פסוק applies
steps.terutzHavaAmina: פרו ורבו applies forever, so they would have had children anyway.
steps.terutzMaskana: פרו ורבו applied only until סיני.

steps.title: Challenge: At Sinai they were told to go back to their tents
steps.stepSummary: Even at סיני‎, ה׳ told the people to return to their tents, meaning their wives. So family life continued after סיני.
steps.simpleTranslation: At סיני it is also written: "Go, say to them: Return to your tents."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second challenge, this time from a פסוק said right at סיני.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in Step 8 was that things changed at סיני. But right after מתן תורה, the men were told to go back to their wives, which looks like married life and children continuing.

phrases.english: At Sinai it is also written:
"Go, say to them:"
phrases.notes: דברים 5:27

phrases.english: "Return to your tents"!
phrases.notes: "Your tents" means your wives. Before מתן תורה they had to stay apart.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּסִינַי נָמֵי כְּתִיב לֵךְ אֱמֹר לָהֶם שׁוּבוּ לָכֶם לְאׇהֳלֵיכֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that having children stopped at סיני
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: At סיני itself they were told to return to their wives, so married life went on.

steps.title: Answer: Returning to their wives was for joy, not for children
steps.stepSummary: Going back to their tents was about the joy of married life, not about having children.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the joy of marital relations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the command was for the happiness of married life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא separates two things: closeness in marriage and having children. ה׳ let them go back to their wives for the joy of it. That does not prove they would have had children.

phrases.english: For the joy of marital relations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reads the פסוק as having a different purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Returning to their tents means they would have children.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was only for the joy of married life, not for children.

steps.title: Challenge: The Torah speaks of good for their children
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק at סיני says it should be good for them and for their children. That seems to mean more children would be born.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: "That it might be good for them and for their children, etc."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third challenge, from another פסוק at סיני that mentions children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ wished goodness for the people at סיני and "their children." If they were going to stop having children, who would those children be?

keyTerms.meaning: so that it may be good

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
"That it might be good for them"
phrases.notes: דברים 5:26

phrases.english: "and for their children, etc."!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another challenge to ריש לקיש and to the idea that having children stopped at סיני.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that without the sin there would be no more children
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק speaks of their children, which sounds like future generations.

steps.title: Answer: Those are the children who stood at Sinai
steps.stepSummary: "Their children" means the children who were already standing at הר סיני, not new ones born later.
steps.simpleTranslation: This refers to those children who were standing at הר סיני.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge, and ריש לקיש's teaching stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The children in the פסוק were already alive and standing at סיני with their parents. So the פסוק does not prove that more children would have been born. All three challenges are answered.
steps.whatToRemember: So far, ריש לקיש's claim that without the sin of the עגל there would have been no children survives three challenges: פרו ורבו applied only until סיני, returning to their tents was for joy, and "their children" were the ones already at סיני. The next steps challenge the claim again, and step 15 changes its wording.

phrases.english: To those who were standing
at Mount Sinai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 11 and closes the back-and-forth.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows who the פסוק is about
steps.terutzMaskana: "Their children" means the children already standing at סיני.

steps.title: אדם הראשון was shown all future generations
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש teaches that הקדוש ברוך הוא showed אדם הראשון every future generation, including רבי עקיבא. So future generations were always planned to exist.
steps.simpleTranslation: But ריש לקיש said: What does the פסוק 'This is the book of the generations of אדם' mean? Did אדם have a book? No. It teaches that ה׳ showed אדם הראשון every generation with its teachers, its sages, and its leaders. When אדם reached רבי עקיבא's generation, he was happy about his תורה and sad about his death. He said: 'How precious to me are Your thoughts, O God.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the earlier idea that without the sin of the עגל, we would never have been born. It brings ריש לקיש's teaching that אדם הראשון saw all future generations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אדם הראשון was already shown רבי עקיבא and the other generations at the beginning of time, those people were always meant to be born. That plan existed long before the sin of the עגל. So how can anyone say we would not have come into the world if they had not sinned?

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't [so-and-so] say? (a formula that opens a challenge)
its expounders (teachers who explain the תורה)

phrases.english: But doesn't Reish Lakish say:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי דִּכְתִיב: ״זֶה סֵפֶר תּוֹלְדֹת אָדָם וְגוֹ׳״?
phrases.english: What is meant by that which is written: "This is the book of the generations of Adam, etc."?
phrases.notes: בראשית 5:1

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי סֵפֶר הָיָה לוֹ לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן?
phrases.english: Did Adam the first man have a book?

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁהֶרְאָה לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
phrases.english: It teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, showed Adam the first man
each generation and its expounders,
each generation and its sages,
each generation and its leaders.

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
phrases.english: When he reached the generation of Rabbi Akiva,
he rejoiced in his Torah and was saddened by his death.
He said: "How precious to me are Your thoughts, O God, etc."
phrases.notes: תהלים 139:17

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling that 'their children' at סיני meant those already alive, the גמרא now challenges the underlying claim that future generations would not have been born.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that had they not sinned, 'we would not have come into the world.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Adam was shown all future generations from the start of Creation, so their birth was always part of the plan, regardless of any sin.

steps.title: משיח comes only after all souls are born
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says בן דוד will not come until all the souls waiting to be born have entered bodies. That means future generations must be born.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי said: בן דוד will not come until all the souls in the 'body' are used up, as the פסוק says: 'For I will not argue forever, nor be angry for all time, for the spirit wraps itself from before Me, and the souls that I have made.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second source to the same challenge. רבי יוסי teaches that משיח needs all the souls to be born first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the גאולה depends on every waiting soul being born, then new generations must come into the world. This again conflicts with the claim that without the sin, no more people would have been born.

keyTerms.meaning: the son of David, meaning משיח
until they are used up or finished
the souls of the 'body,' meaning the souls waiting to be born

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei says:
The son of David does not come
until the souls of the "body" are used up,
phrases.notes: He means that all the souls waiting to come down into bodies must first be born.

phrases.english: as it is said:

phrases.aramaic: ״[כִּי לֹא לְעוֹלָם אָרִיב וְלֹא לָנֶצַח אֶקְּצוֹף]
phrases.english: "For I will not argue forever, nor be angry for all time,"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 57:16. The words in square brackets fill in the beginning of the פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי רוּחַ מִלְּפָנַי יַעֲטוֹף וּנְשָׁמוֹת אֲנִי עָשִׂיתִי״!
phrases.english: "for the spirit wraps itself from before Me, and the souls that I have made"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source to strengthen the challenge from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that had they not sinned, 'we would not have come into the world.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The coming of משיח depends on all souls being born, so future generations are necessary.

steps.title: Not 'we would not exist,' but 'as if we did not exist'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording of the original statement. We would have been born, but it would be as if we never came.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't say 'we would not have come into the world.' Say instead: 'it would be as if we had not come into the world.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers both challenges by reading the original statement differently. Future generations would still be born, just without much importance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier statement is not about whether we exist at all. If the great earlier generations had never died, later people would still be born but would be overshadowed by them. Now there is no conflict with ריש לקיש or רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: do not say (a formula that corrects how a statement is read)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying we would never have been born. It agrees we would be born, only that our place in the world would have seemed small.

phrases.aramaic: לָא תֵּימָא אָנוּ לֹא בָּאנוּ לָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: Do not say "we would not have come into the world,"
rather, "it would be as if we had not come into the world."
phrases.notes: We would still be born, but we would seem unimportant next to the earlier generations who were still alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא תֵּימָא אָנוּ לֹא בָּאנוּ לָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges of steps 13 and 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the original statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The statement meant that later generations would never have been born at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Later generations would be born, but it would be as if they had not come, because they would be overshadowed.

steps.title: Would people never have died? The תורה has laws about death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether people really would never have died without the sin. The תורה contains the laws of יבום and inheritance, which only apply after someone dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that if they had not sinned, they would never have died? But the תורה has the section about יבמות and the section about inheritances!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges the idea underneath all of this: that without the sin, people would have lived forever, like angels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יבום applies only when a husband dies without children, and inheritance applies only when a father dies. If death would never have happened, these sections of the תורה would have no purpose. So it seems death was always expected.

keyTerms.meaning: is this to say? (a formula that draws out what a statement implies, usually to challenge it)
the section about יבום, when a man dies without children

phrases.english: Is this to say that if they had not sinned
they would not have died?
But the section about יבמות is written,
phrases.notes: דברים 25:5-10

phrases.english: and the section about inheritances!
phrases.notes: במדבר 27:8-11

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּאִי לָא חָטְאוּ לָא הֲווֹ מָיְיתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer in step 15, which assumes earlier generations would still be alive, and attacks the idea that there would be no death.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that without the sin of the עגל, people would not have died.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The תורה contains laws that only apply after death, so death must have been expected all along.

steps.title: These sections were written on condition
steps.stepSummary: The laws of יבום and inheritance were written on condition. They would apply only if the people sinned and became mortal.
steps.simpleTranslation: They were written on condition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in two words: those sections were written conditionally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה included laws for a situation that might happen. If the people sinned and death returned, these laws would be needed. Their being written does not prove that death was certain.

phrases.english: Conditionally.
phrases.notes: These laws would only come into use if the people sinned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the purpose of the פסוקים as conditional
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The laws about death show that death was certain.
steps.terutzMaskana: The laws were written for the possibility that the people would sin.

steps.title: Does the תורה write פסוקים on condition?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether it is believable that פסוקים are written for a situation that may never happen.
steps.simpleTranslation: And are פסוקים really written on condition?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer it just gave. Does the תורה really write laws that depend on a condition?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying a פסוק was written 'just in case' is a new idea. The גמרא wants to see that the תורה actually works this way before accepting the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: and is it really so? (a challenging question)

phrases.english: And are verses written conditionally?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the answer of step 17 is believable.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the sections of יבום and inheritance were written on condition.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems unlikely that the תורה would write פסוקים for something that might never happen.

steps.title: All of Creation depended on accepting the תורה
steps.stepSummary: Yes. ריש לקיש teaches that ה׳ made a condition with all of Creation: if ישראל accepts the תורה, good; if not, the world returns to emptiness and chaos.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. This is what רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: What does the פסוק 'And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day' mean? It teaches that ה׳ made a condition with the works of Creation and said: If ישראל accepts the תורה, good. If not, I will return you to emptiness and chaos.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says yes and proves it. The פסוק about the sixth day of Creation hints at a condition placed on the whole world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the whole account of Creation was written under a condition, then other פסוקים can be written that way too. This supports the answer that the laws of יבום and inheritance were written 'just in case.'

keyTerms.meaning: emptiness and chaos, the state before Creation

steps.whatToRemember: We would have been born even without the sin, but it would have been 'as if' we had not come. The laws about death were written on condition, just as all of Creation depended on ישראל accepting the תורה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the existence of the whole world is tied to ישראל accepting the תורה.

phrases.aramaic: אִין, דְּהָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ:
phrases.english: Yes, for this is what Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:
phrases.notes: This is the same person as ריש לקיש.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי דִּכְתִיב ״וַיְהִי עֶרֶב וַיְהִי בֹקֶר יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי״?
phrases.english: What is meant by that which is written: "And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day"?
phrases.notes: בראשית 1:31

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁהִתְנָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עִם מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית,
phrases.english: It teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, made a condition with the works of Creation,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: אִם מְקַבְּלִין יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַתּוֹרָה — מוּטָב,
phrases.english: and said: If Israel accepts the Torah, good;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו — אַחְזִיר אֶתְכֶם לְתוֹהוּ וָבוֹהוּ.
phrases.english: and if not, I will return you to emptiness and chaos.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, דְּהָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18 with a proof that the תורה does speak on condition.
steps.raayaObject: That פסוקים can be written on condition.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's teaching on 'the sixth day': all of Creation was conditional on ישראל accepting the תורה.

steps.title: A ברייתא says death could never have been removed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that even at their highest moment, ישראל could not be freed from מלאך המות. They received the תורה only so that no nation would rule over them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא challenges this from a ברייתא. On the פסוק 'Who would give that they had such a heart,' the ברייתא says it was impossible to remove מלאך המות from them, because the decree had already been made. So ישראל accepted the תורה only so that no nation would rule over them, as it says: 'So that it will be good for them and their children forever.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge ריש לקיש's corrected statement that without the sin, ישראל would never have died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says death was decreed long ago and could not be canceled, even for ישראל at הר סיני. According to the ברייתא, the reward for accepting the תורה was freedom from foreign rule, not freedom from death. That clashes with what ריש לקיש said.

keyTerms.meaning: A nation or language-group, meaning any foreign people

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
"Who would give that they had such a heart"
phrases.notes: דברים 5:26

phrases.english: To cancel the Angel of Death from them
was impossible,
because the decree had already been made.

phrases.aramaic: הָא לֹא קִיבְּלוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַתּוֹרָה
phrases.english: So, Israel did not accept the Torah
phrases.notes: Here הָא means 'so you see,' and it leads into the reason they did accept the תורה.

phrases.english: except so that there would not be
any nation or tongue ruling over them,
as it says: "So that it will be good for them
and for their children forever."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reworded statement of ריש לקיש from step 15 that without the sin they would have been immortal.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's claim that ישראל would never have died had they not sinned.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says death was already decreed and could not be removed. The reward for the תורה was freedom from foreign rule, not immortality.

steps.title: ריש לקיש follows רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש holds like a different תנא, רבי יוסי. He says ישראל accepted the תורה so that מלאך המות would not rule over them.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said his statement like this תנא, as a ברייתא teaches: רבי יוסי says ישראל accepted the תורה only so that מלאך המות would not rule over them. As it says: 'I said, you are godlike, all of you sons of the Most High.' But you ruined your deeds, so: 'Indeed, you will die like a man.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there is a disagreement among תנאים, and ריש לקיש simply follows the opinion of רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not deny the first ברייתא. It shows that another תנא disagrees with it. רבי יוסי reads the פסוק in תהלים as saying ישראל had become like angels who do not die, and they lost this only because of the sin.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this תנא, meaning he follows this opinion

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common way the גמרא defends an אמורא: when a ברייתא contradicts him, it finds a different תנא who agrees with him.

phrases.english: He said it like this tanna,
phrases.notes: 'He' is ריש לקיש. This defends his teaching from step 6, read the way step 15 explained it: without the sin, our ancestors would not have died.

phrases.english: as it was taught: Rabbi Yosei says:
Israel did not accept the Torah
except so that there would not be
the Angel of Death ruling over them,
as it says: "I said: You are godlike,
phrases.notes: תהלים 82:6

phrases.english: and all of you are sons of the Most High."
You ruined your deeds,
phrases.notes: These words aren't in the פסוק. The ברייתא adds them to connect the two פסוקים.

phrases.english: "Indeed, like a man you will die."
phrases.notes: תהלים 82:7

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 by showing that ריש לקיש follows a different תנא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute among תנאים: the challenge comes from one תנא, and ריש לקיש follows the other.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be the only view, so ריש לקיש would be contradicted.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוסי disagrees and holds that the תורה was meant to free ישראל from death. ריש לקיש follows him.

steps.title: How does רבי יוסי read 'so that it will be good'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יוסי explains the פסוק 'so that it will be good for them,' since that seems to promise only goodness while death remains.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי יוסי too, isn't it written, 'So that it will be good for them and their children forever'? That means there would be goodness, but death would still exist!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוסי with the same פסוק the first ברייתא used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק promises 'good,' not 'life forever.' That sounds like death stays in place, which seems to go against רבי יוסי's view that the תורה would have removed death.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei as well,
isn't it written: "So that it will be good for them
and for their children forever"?
It is goodness that there will be,
but death there still is!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוסי, who was brought in step 21, using the פסוק quoted in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי's view that accepting the תורה would have removed death.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק only promises goodness, which suggests death would still exist.

steps.title: No death is the greatest good
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי would answer that the 'good' in the פסוק is living forever, since nothing is better than that.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי would tell you: since there is no death, there is no greater good than this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי יוסי by explaining what 'good' in the פסוק really means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'good' does not mean only something less than immortality. The greatest good possible is not dying, so 'good forever' itself means eternal life. That way the פסוק supports רבי יוסי instead of challenging him.

keyTerms.meaning: He would say to you (an answer on someone's behalf)

steps.whatToRemember: Two views of what ישראל gained from accepting the תורה: (1) the first ברייתא says freedom from foreign rule, because death was already decreed; (2) רבי יוסי says freedom from death, which is the greatest 'good.' ריש לקיש follows רבי יוסי.

phrases.english: (Rabbi Yosei) would say to you:
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the name in round brackets, but either way the speaker is רבי יוסי.

phrases.english: Since there is no death,
there is no greater good than this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22 by reading 'good' as eternal life.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Good' sounded like something less than immortality, with death still existing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'good' is itself the absence of death, the greatest good there is.

steps.title: Challenging the first opinion from 'You shall die like a man'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the תנא קמא, who holds that ישראל were never freed from death, explains the פסוק 'אכן כאדם תמותון'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the first תנא too, isn't it written: 'Yet you shall die like a man'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the other side. It challenges the תנא קמא, who said ישראל were never freed from מלאך המות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'you shall die like a man' sounds like death was a new punishment that came after the sin. That suggests that before the sin, ישראל could have lived forever. This goes against the תנא קמא, who said they were never freed from death.

keyTerms.meaning: The first (unnamed) opinion in a ברייתא or משנה

phrases.english: And according to the first תנא too,
phrases.notes: This is the תנא from Step 20, who said ישראל could not be freed from מלאך המות.

phrases.english: isn't it written: "Yet you shall die like a man"?
phrases.notes: תהלים 82:7. It sounds like dying was a new punishment, so before the sin they could have lived forever.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Just as Steps 22-23 challenged רבי יוסי from a פסוק, this step challenges the other side, the תנא קמא, from a פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The תנא קמא's view that ישראל were never freed from מלאך המות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק makes death sound like a new punishment, which suggests that before the sin they were free of death.

steps.title: Death here means poverty
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא answers that the 'death' in the פסוק is not real death but poverty.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'death'? Poverty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for the תנא קמא: the word 'die' in this פסוק does not mean real death. It means becoming poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'die' means becoming poor, the פסוק no longer proves that ישראל were ever free of real death. The punishment for the sin was poverty, not losing eternal life. So the תנא קמא's view stays standing.

phrases.english: What is meant by "death"?
Poverty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 24 by reading the word 'death' in a different way.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'You shall die' means real death, so ישראל must once have been free from death.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'You shall die' means becoming poor, so the פסוק says nothing about being free from real death.

steps.title: Four people are considered like dead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports reading 'death' as poverty with a teaching that four kinds of people are considered like dead, and a poor person is one of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Master said: Four are considered like dead people: a poor person, a blind person, a מצורע, and one who has no children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the answer: a known teaching says a poor person is counted as if he were dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since a poor person is called 'like dead', it makes sense that a פסוק could use the word 'die' to mean becoming poor. The teaching lists four such people, and the next steps give a פסוק for each one.
steps.whatToRemember: Four are considered like dead: a poor person, a blind person, a מצורע, and one with no children.

phrases.english: As the Master said:
Four are considered like dead people,
these are: a poor person, a blind person,
and a מצורע, and one who has no children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of Step 25 that 'death' can mean poverty.
steps.raayaObject: That 'death' in the פסוק can mean poverty.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A teaching (מר) that four types of people, including the poor, are considered like dead.

steps.title: The source for a poor person: דתן and אבירם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a פסוק for a poor person being like dead: ה׳ told משה that the men who wanted to kill him 'have died', meaning דתן and אבירם.
steps.simpleTranslation: A poor person, as it is written: 'For all the men have died.' And who were they? דתן and אבירם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts giving a פסוק for each of the four. First is the poor person, from a פסוק about דתן and אבירם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ told משה he could go back to מצרים because the men who wanted to kill him had 'died'. The גמרא identifies those men as דתן and אבירם. This sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Two men who fought against משה

phrases.english: A poor person — as it is written:
"For all the men have died"
phrases.notes: שמות 4:19, said to משה about the men who wanted to kill him.

phrases.english: And who were they? דתן and אבירם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts giving the sources for the four listed in Step 26, beginning with the poor person.
steps.raayaObject: That a poor person is considered like dead.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 4:19, 'כי מתו כל האנשים', said about דתן and אבירם.

steps.title: But דתן and אבירם were still alive
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: did דתן and אבירם really die? They were still alive later!
steps.simpleTranslation: But did they die? They were alive!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a problem: דתן and אבירם did not actually die at that time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דתן and אבירם were still around years later, in the time of קרח. So the word 'died' in the פסוק cannot mean real death. This sets up the answer that it means something else.

phrases.english: But did they die? They were alive!
phrases.notes: They were still alive years later, when they joined קרח against משה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the plain meaning of the פסוק brought in Step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading 'מתו' in שמות 4:19 as real death.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: דתן and אבירם were alive later, so they could not have really died then.

steps.title: They lost their property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'died' means they lost their wealth and became poor, which proves a poor person is like dead.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means that they lost their property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'died' here means דתן and אבירם became poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since they did not really die, the תורה must be calling their poverty 'death'. This proves that a poor person is considered like dead, which is exactly what Step 26 claimed.

phrases.english: Rather, it means that they lost their property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 28 and completes the proof for the poor person.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the פסוק
steps.terutzMaskana: 'מתו' means they became poor, so a poor person is called dead.

steps.title: Sources for the blind person, the מצורע, and the childless
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a פסוק for each of the other three: a blind person, a מצורע, and one without children.
steps.simpleTranslation: A blind person, as it is written: 'He has made me sit in dark places, like those long dead.' A מצורע, as it is written: 'Let her not be like a dead person.' And one who has no children, as it is written: 'Give me children, and if not, I am dead.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the list by giving one פסוק each for the blind person, the מצורע, and someone with no children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each פסוק compares that person to someone dead. Darkness is compared to the long dead, מרים's צרעת is called being 'like a dead person', and רחל said she was like dead without children. This completes the support for the teaching in Step 26.
steps.whatToRemember: Every one of the four 'like dead' people has its own פסוק. For the poor person, it is the פסוק about דתן and אבירם.

phrases.english: A blind person — as it is written:
"He has made me sit in dark places, like those long dead."
phrases.notes: איכה 3:6

phrases.english: A מצורע — as it is written:
"Please, let her not be like a dead person."
phrases.notes: במדבר 12:12, said by אהרן when מרים got צרעת.

phrases.english: And one who has no children — as it is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״הָבָה לִּי בָנִים וְאִם אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי״.
phrases.english: "Give me children, and if not, I am dead."
phrases.notes: בראשית 30:1, said by רחל to יעקב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of sources begun in Step 27 for the remaining three people.
steps.raayaObject: That a blind person, a מצורע, and a childless person are considered like dead.

steps.title: 'If' in 'If you walk in My laws' is a plea
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the word 'אם' in 'אם בחקתי תלכו' is a word of pleading, as if ה׳ is begging ישראל to keep the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'If you walk in My laws.' The word 'if' here is only a word of pleading.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new teaching. A ברייתא says that the 'if' in 'אם בחקתי תלכו' is not just a condition but ה׳ pleading with ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally 'if' just sets a condition. Here the ברייתא says it expresses a wish, as if ה׳ is hoping ישראל will keep His laws. This fits the earlier theme of ה׳ wanting ישראל to accept the תורה.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not saying that keeping the תורה is optional. It is saying that the word 'if' shows how much ה׳ wants ישראל to keep it.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"If you walk in My laws"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 26:3

phrases.english: the word "if" here is only a word of pleading.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching. It fits the theme of ה׳ hoping ישראל would accept and keep the תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'אם' in 'אם בחקתי תלכו' means ה׳ is pleading, not just setting a condition.

steps.title: Two more פסוקים showing ה׳'s plea
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings two פסוקים where ה׳ says 'if only' My people would listen, showing the same pleading tone.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says: 'If only My people would listen to Me, I would quickly subdue their enemies.' And it says: 'If only you had listened to My commandments, your peace would be like a river, and your children would be like the sand.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא supports its point with two פסוקים where ה׳ clearly wishes that ישראל would listen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both פסוקים the word 'לו' means 'if only', which is a clear wish. ה׳ lists the good things He would give if ישראל would listen. This shows that 'אם' in בחקתי has the same wishing, pleading tone.
steps.whatToRemember: ה׳'s 'if' in the תורה is a loving plea: He wants ישראל to keep His laws so He can give them good.

phrases.english: And so it says:
"If only My people would listen to Me [etc.]
phrases.notes: תהלים 81:14-15. 'לו' means 'if only', a clear wish, and that's the point of the proof.

phrases.english: I would quickly subdue their enemies."
And it says:
"If only you had listened to My commandments,
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 48:18-19

phrases.english: your peace would be like a river, etc.,

phrases.aramaic: וַיְהִי כַחוֹל זַרְעֶךָ וְצֶאֱצָאֵי מֵעֶיךָ וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: and your children would be like the sand, and the offspring of your body, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: לוּ עַמִּי שׁוֹמֵעַ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim of Step 31 with parallel פסוקים.
steps.raayaObject: That 'אם' in 'אם בחקתי תלכו' is a word of pleading.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים 81:14-15 and ישעיהו 48:18-19, both using 'לו' (if only).

steps.title: משה calls ישראל ingrates for not saying 'You give it'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that when הקב״ה said 'If only they had such a heart,' ישראל should have answered 'You give it to us!' Because they did not, משה called them ingrates, children of ingrates.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught about the פסוק 'Who would give that they had such a heart as this': משה said to ישראל, 'Ingrates, children of ingrates!' When הקב״ה said to ישראל, "Who would give that they had such a heart as this," they should have said: You give it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about the פסוק 'מי יתן'. It says ישראל missed a chance to ask הקב״ה to give them a heart that fears Him, and משה criticized them for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מי יתן' literally means 'Who would give?', a way of saying 'If only.' The ברייתא reads it as an opening: הקב״ה Himself is the One who can give, so ישראל should have answered 'You give!' Not asking is called being כפויי טובה, ungrateful.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'Who would give?' It means 'If only'
Ingrates: people who do not recognize the good done for them
'You give!': the answer ישראל should have given

steps.confusionAlert: משה is not saying ישראל had to fear ה׳ completely on their own. His complaint is that they should have asked הקב״ה to give them that heart.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"Who would give that they had such a heart as this"
phrases.notes: דברים 5:26. 'Who would give' is a way of saying 'If only.'

phrases.english: Moshe said to the Jewish people:
Ingrates, children of ingrates!

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל:
phrases.english: At the time that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to the Jewish people:
"Who would give that they had such a heart as this"
they should have said: You give it!
phrases.notes: They should have asked ה׳ to give them that heart to fear Him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מִי יִתֵּן וְהָיָה לְבָבָם זֶה לָהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the pleading פסוקים in Steps 31-32, the גמרא opens a new ברייתא on another 'if only' פסוק, 'מי יתן', and reads it as a missed chance for ישראל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When הקב״ה said 'מי יתן', ישראל should have answered 'תן אתה'. Because they did not, משה called them כפויי טובה בני כפויי טובה.

steps.title: Source that ישראל were ingrates: complaining about the מן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to bring a פסוק proving that ישראל were ingrates, quoting their complaint 'And our soul loathes' about the מן.
steps.simpleTranslation: They were ingrates, as it is written: 'And our soul loathes...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to show where we see that ישראל were 'ingrates.' It quotes the first words of the פסוק where they complained about the מן, and the quote continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה used a strong word, 'ingrates.' Now the גמרא backs it up from a פסוק. ישראל received the מן as a gift from heaven, yet they said their souls were disgusted by it. That is a clear picture of not appreciating good.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written: introduces a פסוק as a source
And our soul loathes: ישראל's complaint about the מן

phrases.english: They were ingrates, as it is written:
"And our soul loathes
phrases.notes: במדבר 21:5. They are complaining about the מן, and the פסוק continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the first half of משה's words in Step 33, 'כפויי טובה', with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That ישראל were כפויי טובה, as משה called them
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 21:5, 'ונפשנו קצה בלחם הקלקל', where ישראל complain about the מן
